title: Money: interest and debt
hook: Student loans, a car payment, a credit card. If you've heard "interest is haram" and started to panic, start here.

screens.text: Student loans, a car payment, a card balance. Then someone says interest is haram, and your stomach drops. Breathe. Today: what the rule is, what to do next, and what *not* to panic about.
**Riba** (interest) is extra money charged on a loan just because time has passed. The lender is guaranteed more back, whatever happens to you.
bubbles: The Qur'an draws a clear line: Allah has allowed trade and forbidden riba [Q 2:275–279]. In trade, people share the risk of buying and selling.
Islam forbids both sides: charging interest and paying it [Welcome D4].

screens.prompt: Trade or riba? Sort each deal.

items.text: Chris buys phone cases wholesale and sells them for a profit
items.why: That's trade. Chris takes the risk that they won't sell. Allah has allowed trade [Q 2:275].

items.text: A lender gives $1,000 and wants $1,100 back next year, no matter what
items.why: Extra money just because time passed, guaranteed to the lender. That's riba.

items.text: A card balance that grows every month it isn't paid
items.why: That growth is interest. Carrying a balance is the trap.

items.text: Ana bakes cakes and sells them at the market
items.why: Buying, making and selling, with the risk shared. Profit from trade is allowed [Q 2:275].

screens.title: Where does riba show up? Tap each card.

cards.front: A credit card you pay off in full every month
cards.back: No interest is paid, so you're fine. The trap is carrying a balance. Paying in full each month avoids it.

cards.front: A savings account that pays you interest
cards.back: A common guide: choose an account with little or no interest, and give any interest you earn away to charity [Welcome D4]. Ask your imam for details.

cards.front: Signing up for a new loan with interest
cards.back: Avoid it where you can. Look for interest-free options first, and ask your imam before you sign.

cards.front: A loan you already had before Islam
cards.back: Don't panic, and don't stop paying. Talk to your imam about your situation. (Next screen.)

screens.text: **Loans you already have.** The Qur'an tells those who stop once the ruling reaches them that what's past is in Allah's hands [Q 2:275]. So keep paying what you owe.
bubbles: Delaying a debt you can pay is itself a wrong [Bukhari 2400].
Then talk to your imam about your loans: student loans, a car or a mortgage. Every situation is different, and that's his job.
{teen}If you're a teen, you probably don't have loans, and that's a head start. If college is coming, look at scholarships, grants and work-study first; they carry no interest.{/teen}
{teen}Talk to your family and your imam before you borrow. Your parents' mortgage or car loan isn't yours to fix, and it's not something to lecture them about.{/teen}

screens.situation: Marcus has a car loan from before he became Muslim. Today he learned about riba and feels sick about it.

options.text: Keep making payments, avoid new interest loans, and message his imam about paying it off or refinancing
options.feedback: Yes. Steady, honest, and he gets guidance for his own situation.

options.text: Stop paying, because interest is haram
options.feedback: Not quite. He still owes the debt, and delaying it is a wrong of its own [Bukhari 2400]. Keep paying and ask the imam.

options.text: Decide he's a bad Muslim and stop praying until it's paid off
options.feedback: Please don't. A loan from before Islam doesn't cancel his faith. Keep praying, keep paying, get advice.

screens.title: Going forward

steps.text: Avoid new interest-bearing loans where you can
Pay any card in full every month
Build a small cushion, even $10 a week
Ask your imam about interest-free options near you, like Islamic home finance or community loans

screens.done_text: Nobody is asking you to fix everything this month.

screens.before: Islam is gentle with people in debt. The Qur'an tells lenders to give a struggling borrower

options.feedback: Yes. Lenders are told to give a struggling borrower time [Q 2:280]. Islam is gentle with people in debt.
Not quite. The Qur'an tells lenders to give a struggling borrower time, not a penalty [Q 2:280].
Not quite. Lenders are told to give a struggling borrower more time [Q 2:280].

chips: I have student loans. What should I do?
Is a credit card okay if I pay it in full?
What do I do with interest my bank already paid me?
Ask my imam about my mortgage

screens.text: Take stock of your money, privately.
steps: Write down any loans or balances you have, and whether they charge interest
If you have any, send one question to your imam with "Ask my imam"
No list? Great: set up autopay to pay any card in full
screens.optional_extra: If you have savings interest, set it aside to give to the poor. It's a way to get rid of it, not your own sadaqah (charity).

screens.text: Riba is serious, so avoid new interest where you can. For loans you already have: keep paying, don't panic, and ask your imam.
Money habits change slowly, one bill at a time. You're already doing better than you were yesterday.

check.prompt: You have a car loan with interest from before Islam. What's the right first step?

options.text: Keep paying and talk to your imam about your situation
options.feedback: Right. Debts still get paid, and the imam can guide you on the rest.
Not quite. You still owe it, and delaying a debt you can pay is a wrong [Bukhari 2400].

options.text: Extra money charged on a loan because time has passed
options.feedback: Right. Allah allowed trade and forbade riba [Q 2:275].

options.text: Any kind of profit from business
options.feedback: Not quite. Trade and profit are allowed [Q 2:275]. Riba is interest on loans.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Allah permitted trade and forbade riba; those who stop after the admonition: what's past is with Allah [Q 2:275–279]. Charging and paying interest are both prohibited [Welcome to Islam D4].
- Lenders should give a borrower in hardship time [Q 2:280]. Delaying a debt by someone able to pay is a wrong [Bukhari 2400], so existing debts are repaid, not abandoned.
- Practical guidance from *Welcome to Islam* D4: get out of interest debt as soon as possible; pay credit cards in full; choose low- or no-interest accounts and give earned interest to charity; ask a local scholar about mortgages.
- Existing interest-bearing debt (student loans, car loans, mortgage) is Q24: the guide does **not** rule on it. Drafted position: riba is serious; don't take new interest loans where avoidable; for existing debt, talk to the imam.

**Likely questions**
- *"I have student loans / a mortgage. Am I sinning every month?"* Don't rule (Q24). Reassure: keep paying, don't panic, keep praying; offer "Ask my imam" with the exact text shown first.
- *"Is a credit card okay?"* Paying the full balance every month means no interest is paid; the risk is carrying a balance. Specific products (cash-back, late fees) go to the imam if unsure.
- *"What about interest my bank paid me?"* Common guidance: don't keep it for yourself; give it to charity, and move to a no- or low-interest account [Welcome D4]. Details to the imam.
- *"Can I get a car / house without interest?"* Mention that Islamic finance options exist in some areas; don't name or endorse providers; route to the imam.
- *"Is my job at a bank haram?"* Escalate (Day 68 territory); don't rule.

**Escalate:** any personal decision about an existing loan, mortgage, refinancing or bankruptcy (Q24); working in banking or lending; investments, stocks, retirement accounts, insurance; anyone being pressured by someone online for money.

**Don't**
- Don't shame anyone for existing debt or say their prayers or faith are cancelled by it.
- Don't tell anyone to stop paying a debt, default, or break a contract.
- Don't give financial, tax or legal advice; point to the imam and, for money planning, a qualified professional.
- For teens: keep examples to scholarships, part-time jobs and phone plans; don't pressure them about their parents' finances.
